extracted.intended_audience: young newspaper reporters / journalism students / cub reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing clear, forceful news stories — especially interviews, speeches, courts — including word choice, lead types, handling quotations, fairness, and use of figures and mannerisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misuse of words / precise word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader should distinguish keenly between each pair of words and should be careful never to misuse one of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive lists of commonly misused, pretentious, or inappropriate words are provided — prefer simple everyday words (home vs residence, begin vs commence, coffin vs casket). Do not use affectations or wrong synonyms; consult the provided lists and a standard dictionary when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure interest, a word must be clear and forceful; it should not be technical or big, but simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the simplest words — everyday Anglo-Saxon vocabulary — because the average newspaper reader has a limited vocabulary and will not look up unfamiliar words. Simplicity = force + brevity; avoid ornate, technical, or little-known words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force (use of emphatic, specific wording)
rubrics_metrics.description: Force demands that one's words be emphatic, fitting, apt, fresh, unhackneyed, and specific rather than general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose specific terms (e.g., 'ten thousand persons' rather than 'a vast concourse' or 'about ten thousand'). When given a choice, use the specific term. Avoid vague qualifiers like 'about' when a round specific is effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trite phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek originality of expression and avoid trite phraseology and hackneyed words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freshness must be found day after day; do not rely on conventional stock phrases (e.g., 'the bride was elegantly gowned', 'tripped the light fantastic'). Strive for a new way to tell familiar events and resist 'embalmed meats' and 'kyanized sentences.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures of speech — use cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of speech add suggestiveness and increase meaning but must be used carefully to avoid mixing metaphors or producing incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An apt figure can be more effective than a literal description, but do not mix figures or personify names of ships, cities, states, and countries. Examples of bad mixing are given. Ensure figurative language is apt and consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance (usage and formality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Force requires attention to trivialities of good usage: correct titles, avoidance of coinage of titles, and restrained pronoun use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to clergy as 'the Rev. Mr. Anderson,' not 'Rev. Anderson.' Do not invent titles ('Railway Inspector Brown') in place of proper descriptions. Avoid the editorial 'we' in news articles; unsigned stories should not use 'I' or stilted circumlocutions; signed stories may use 'I' more freely but avoid archaic self-descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slang — limit use
rubrics_metrics.description: Slang is barred from most columns because of lack of elegance and clearness; it is acceptable in narrow contexts like sporting pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use slang only where the audience understands it (e.g., sporting pages). Regional or ephemeral slang may confuse readers elsewhere. New coinages may be admitted (burglarize, home-run, diner) but avoid dubious terms (glad rags, bagging, swiping, enthuse) and consult a dictionary if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the main types of news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: For beginners, most news stories reduce to a handful of types for practical handling: interviews, accidents, society, and sports (plus rewrites, feature stories, correspondence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify stories for approach and handling; many apparently different events (automobile collision, fire) can be grouped (e.g., accidents). Understanding types helps determine method of handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead to an interview — choice of feature
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead to a personal-interview news story may feature: (i) the name of the person interviewed, (ii) a direct statement from him, (iii) an indirect statement, (iv) the general topic, (v) the occasion, or (vi) the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If featuring the name, begin with the speaker’s name and locate the conversation in time/place; if a significant statement dominates, lead with the statement then give speaker, time, place, and occasion. Examples provided illustrate best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature statements of local interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead the person interviewed to comment on topics of local interest and feature those statements, especially if they align with a declared policy of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask visitors for opinions on civic/state/national issues (commission government, prohibition, tariff, preparedness). A prominent figure's neutral statement on a local issue is a valuable, evidently unbiased feature; newspapers may emphasize or ignore such statements depending on alignment with editorial policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiring about the feature (ask what to develop)
rubrics_metrics.description: Often the feature for the lead may be found by asking the interviewee what he would like brought out or developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a courtesy when the interviewee is generous, but reporters should very rarely submit copy for approval before publication — doing so risks losing the story's piquancy and invites repudiation by the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in the interview
rubrics_metrics.description: The interviewer's first aims must be fairness, accuracy, and absence of personal bias; the interview can be abused as an unfair weapon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not color a person's opinions or editorialize on them. Legitimately break into quotations to explain speaker meaning or elaborate possible effects, and if a speaker should be challenged, obtain and quote a reply from a local prominent person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain logical sequence and proportion of ideas so the printed interview presents thought and spirit, regardless of the order or length given by the interviewee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regroup and develop ideas when interviewees overemphasize trivial points or introduce the important point late; ensure ideas follow logically in the printed version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying the person interviewed
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide explanatory paragraphs about the person and how he came to grant the interview so readers understand his position and right to be heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many readers do not know prominent names; dwell on rank, position, reputation, or relevant background to inspire reader confidence in the subject's statements. Examples illustrate biographical/contextual paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling conversation (condense and quote selectively)
rubrics_metrics.description: Condense where possible: give the pith of prolix parts in a sentence or two, then resume direct quotation when the speaker becomes interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to report everything said; avoid a Q&A cut-and-dried format. Prefer a succession of personal paragraphs with direct statements, but quote exact language when the manner of saying matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mannerisms and incidental description
rubrics_metrics.description: Liven reports with descriptive bits portraying the speaker and surroundings — mannerisms, gestures, characteristic phrases — to convey atmosphere and spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpolate pet phrases, gestures, sudden anger, reticence, or other details at intervals; these incidentals can be more effective than columns of quotation in presenting the interview's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons refusing to talk — report the foiled interview
rubrics_metrics.description: If an interviewer fails to get access or make the subject talk, still produce a story by narrating the foiled efforts or quoting the questions refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foiled-interview stories can be powerful when the reporter notes demeanor, noncommittal replies, and surrounding circumstances; such inference can scoop other correspondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of inference in foiled interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: A skilled reporter can produce a significant story from very few facts by playing up small details and making judicious inferences from demeanor and incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how minor, seemingly trivial incidents (facial expressions, perspiration, avoidance) suggest larger events; use rare judgment and accurate observation to turn sparse facts into a compelling narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series of interviews — structuring and naming
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story contains multiple interviews, let the lead feature the consensus and present individual quotations with each man's name prominently at paragraph start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For many interviews, set the name in display type at paragraph beginning so readers can scan changes between speakers; if interviewees are not prominent but worth quoting, embed names within paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads for speeches — multiple options
rubrics_metrics.description: A speech report lead may feature: (i) the speaker's theme, (ii) the title of the address, (iii) a forceful direct quotation, (iv) an indirect dynamic statement, (v) the speaker's name, (vi) the occasion, or (vii) the time/place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the lead form that best conveys the address's import. For sermons and lectures, typewritten copies are often available; if you took good notes you can select any of these approaches depending on what will most interest readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featuring a single sentence from a speech
rubrics_metrics.description: A quotation of a single sentence or paragraph is effective if it gives the keynote of the speech or harmonizes with the paper's policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick a forceful sentence that encapsulates the address's theme or aligns with editorial stance; examples show how a single memorable line makes an effective lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playing up random statements that support paper policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Play up even a random statement in the lead if it happens to agree with a specific policy or campaign of the paper; ignore those opposed to the paper's views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A speaker's offhand remark touching politics or civic topics can be an excellent, evidently unbiased feature. Use such statements selectively according to the paper's editorial commitments; they are valuable because they appear unmotivated.
